In 2021, Vauhini Vara asked OpenAI’s GPT-3 to help her write about her sister. Since her sister’s death, Vara hadn’t been able to do it herself. The then-emerging technology offered an unusual path through the block.

This was pre-ChatGPT and the resulting text was novel: a piece titled "Ghosts: I didn’t know how to write about my sister’s death—so I had AI do it for me." Vara’s words were published in bold, with GPT-3’s contributions beneath in Courier New. Littered throughout were what we now call hallucinations: AI-generated responses that contain something false presented as fact. But, as the story unfurled, the bold sections lengthened, with the final chapter almost entirely made up of Vara’s own words.

Illustration by Jesse Zhan, source: Ghosts by Vauhini Vara

The last paragraph was stirring:**** “**Once upon a time, my sister taught me to read. She taught me to wait for a mosquito to swell on my arm and then slap it and see the blood spurt out. She taught me to insult racists back. To swim. To pronounce English so I sounded less Indian. To shave my legs without cutting myself. To lie to our parents believably.**_To do math. To tell stories. Once upon a time, she taught me to exist.”_

Vara had worked through her grief with the language model, and shared that working with the world. At the time, it was provocative – today, sharing your chatbot interactions is becoming something more practical. It’s proof of effort. In the same way, pop stars are pulling the curtain back on their creative processes, like Charli xcx via her Substack or Lorde dropping a 49-track release of raw recording sessions. Brands too are going to great lengths to prove their marketing is human-made – Apple TV’s new logo was made with sheets of glass and Google’s Mother’s Day doodle used a real baby’s hand. Taking things a step further, people have started publishing their conversations with AI.

Last year, Venkatesh Rao launched the “Sloptraptions” section of his Substack. As a companion to his internet-famous Contraptions newsletter, the posts go out twice a week and are written in collaboration with AI; Rao calls it “elevated slop”. Initially, he ended each post with a “recipe”, detailing how the “co-authoring protocol” worked. And, in at least one instance, he linked out to his conversation with ChatGPT.

Clicking the link was like accepting an invitation into Rao’s brain. It was intimate, and reading the transcript was far more interesting than the final AI-generated product. I almost didn’t care about what Chat was writing; I was looking at the questions Rao was asking, the adjustments he was making along the way, the way he was thinking.

A new series from Substack – Model Behavior – pulls on the same strings. The inaugural issue, published at the end of July, announced “we’ll ask each guest to give us a behind-the-scenes look at their creative process […] we’ll get into the prompts they choose, their tool stacks, or their 100% analog workflows.” The first guest, prominent tech journalist and meme lord, Taylor Lorenz, shared that she spends about $300 per month on AI tools and detailed how they feature in her day-to-day work, including the exact 364-word prompt she feeds five separate models to get title and thumbnail suggestions for her podcast episodes.

Lorenz likely has no ulterior motives for sharing these details. Still, seeing how much work she puts into squeezing the most out of these models could shift things a little. AI may not seem like such an easy shortcut when you quantify the amount of effort that goes into using it. And arguably, as AI detection tools become more commonplace – such as Pangram and Substack’s recent partnership – transparency over LLM usage could become a necessity.

While you don’t want to get caught “Claudefishing” – passing off AI-generated prose as your own – the most exciting element of these prompt receipts is the glimpse they give into thought processes: a whole new genre of content, a new depth of understanding. Whose brains could we peek into next? Bobbi Brown discussing colour theory with ChatGPT? Ralph Lauren debating Claude on English versus American style? Ronald McDonald arguing with Grok over the McRib?

Software developer Dave Griffith compares this to the documentary film _No Maps For These Territories_ , a rambling conversation with science fiction author William Gibson conducted from the back of a limo rolling around Singapore. “I recently realized I would pay real money for a fifty-page chatbot transcript produced by William Gibson and Claude,” Griffith writes on his Substack. “Not an interview, not an essay, not a novel — a raw working session where Gibson is thinking through whatever he’s currently obsessed with, with an inhuman interlocutor that can keep pace and push into interesting territory.”

His interest in this imagined artefact is similar to my interest in Rao’s conversations with ChatGPT: he wants to see Gibson’s mind move. “Here’s what makes the shared transcript genuinely different from every communication medium that preceded it: it transmits thinking, not thoughts,” Griffith writes. “A transcript is a cognitive portrait in a way that no finished work can be.”

external.description:
Young people are apparently not having sex, or dating, or drinking, or going clubbing. Every other person – well, 1 in 8 Americans – is on Ozempic. And looksmaxxing is pushing beauty practices to dangerous extremes, emphasising attractiveness that’s online-approved over fulfilment that’s physically-felt. Looking around, we seem to find ourselves in the midst of a pleasure recession.

Our bodies were once thought of as centres for sensory delight, yet they’re now largely seen as systems to optimise and invest in, discussed in the co-opted language of venture capital. A piece published in The Guardian last month defined this state of joyless self-indulgence as the “era of decadence without pleasure”. A culture that views restraint as a virtue to flex.

Across human history, bliss has sprung from two primary sources: food and sex. Both release powerful chemicals into our bloodstream: dopamine, endorphins and oxytocin igniting sensations that span euphoria to serenity. But new technology threatens these organic systems, interrupting them with ensnaring loops of shallow, synthetic delights.

Detail from Hieronymus Bosch's The Garden of Earthly Delights (circa 1490 and 1510)

We fill ourselves up, yet still crave more. The answer to enduring, satiating pleasure is delayed gratification and an intentional pursuit of it. A theme we explored in our Spring 2026 BRIEFING, outlining how brands can re-introduce friction to spark more rewarding experiences.

Pleasure can be simple, like little treat culture, or grand, like extravagant summers spent on the Côte d’Azur. But what’s increasingly apparent is that pleasure has become more about self-obsession than collective joy. Brands occupy a powerful position to relight the fire.

### **The Big Eroticism Shortage**

The psychotherapist Esther Perel’s book, _Mating in Captivity,_ reflects the pattern that she’d kept encountering in her practice: couples, very much in love, but not physically intimate. 20 years on, data shows this dwindling flame has only spread. According to the Institute for Family Studies, weekly sexual activity among U.S. adults fell from 55% in 1990 to 37% in 2024, while 24% of 18 to 29 year olds had no sex at all in the past year, doubling since 2010.

But Perel doesn’t think reading into “unsexy” statistics is the solution. She proposes there’s something larger at play: an eroticism shortage, to borrow from Faith Hill in The Atlantic. As Hill explains, “erotic” can encompass sex, but it’s more of “a state one enters into when they’re playful, intrigued, open to the unknown.” Several of the strategies in the Protein Stupid REPORT echo this, proposing how brands can facilitate curiosity, exploration and spontaneity – relief from a tightly clenched culture.

The age-old saying “sex sells” defined the pin-ups of the 1940s, stripped-down Calvin Klein campaigns of the ‘90s and lewd Lynx ads of the 2000s, heavily implying that their products would make you wildly irresistible. Fantasy and desire in marketing will always play their part, even if the misogyny is now less blatant, but brands must refresh this strategy for a more expansive and inclusive approach to sex. Dating apps such as Feeld, and their newly-launched Reflections quiz, potently embody this. Tinder also recently rebranded for the first time in almost a decade to clarify its position in today's dating landscape.

Reflections by Feeld

Perhaps most interesting shift comes from what Raquel S. Benedict surmised of today’s culture: “Everyone is beautiful and no one is horny”. In her 2021 piece for Blood Knife, Benedict assesses the simultaneous fetishisation and de-sexualisation of the body. “Even when they have sex, no one is horny. No one is attracted to anyone else,” she observes of contemporary cinema. “No one is hungry for anyone else.” The total absence of sex in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey – despite the original tale being packed full of it – is in keeping with what Benedict describes as the director’s “inexplicably sexless oeuvre”.

The physical intimacy crisis has become so dire that Stück, a café-cum-co-working space-cum-club, in Dalston, is encouraging its members to consummate between meetings. Described by some as a mix of “ yoga and Berghain”, Stück costs £45 a month and includes complimentary tea, coffee and condoms.

external.description:
In his 1983 book, Frames of the Mind, Howard Gardner – professor of cognition and education of Harvard University – challenged the notion of intelligence as something singular. Instead, his Theory of Multiple Intelligences proposed that intelligence manifests in eight different ways, which each of us possess to varying degrees. Intelligence, and in turn stupidity, is broader and more diffused than we’d been taught. One of these forms of intelligence is physical: a deep connection with our bodies and celebration of their form.

As our Stupid REPORT outlines, intelligence and stupidity are two sides of the same coin; playing into the absurd and surprising might be the smartest thing brands can do right now. The two case studies below demonstrate how brands can be successfully stupid.

* * *

## I Wanna Bangkok

Thailand based fashion brand I Wanna Bangkok have followed their creative impulses from the very start, pushing aside any structured business plans. Their products were initially designed to target tourists but accidentally ended up appealing to Thai youths who were finally seeing queer culture celebrated, not fetishised, by those outside it. The brand doesn’t restrict themselves just to clothes: pop-ups, food collaborations and filmmaking come together to build a 360 sensory world that feeds the imaginations of their fiercely loyal and imaginative audience.

I Wanna Bangkok embraces an anarchic approach that’s visceral, like asymmetric underpants or gym bro t-shirts illustrated with ripped bodies and impressive packages. Partnering with Thai ice cream specialist Kintaam, they created a three-boob dessert. A delicious blend of sexy and stupid.

I Wanna Bangkok x Kintaam

The brand exists in a potent moment, with buzz building around those who dare to experiment and resist acclimatising to the monoculture that social media and AI enforce.

Cisco Patches Multiple Critical Cisco IOS XE Software Vulnerabilities – Patch Now!

external.description:
Cisco has released a critical security hardening update for Cisco IOS XE Software, fixing several serious vulnerabilities that could expose enterprise network devices to remote attacks. 



 The advisory covers vulnerabilities identified during Cisco’s internal security testing, including testing supported by frontier AI models. 



 Cisco said it is not aware of public exploitation or malicious activity linked to these flaws. However, the severity of the issues, combined with the lack of available workarounds, makes prompt patching essential. 



 The vulnerabilities affect Cisco IOS XE Software running in autonomous mode or controller mode, regardless of device configuration. Cisco assessed releases 17.9, 17.12, 17.15, 17.18, and 26.1 as part of this review. Cisco Catalyst 3650 and 3850 Series Switches were not evaluated because they do not run the reviewed releases. 



 The most severe issue is CVE-2026-20272, which carries a maximum CVSS score of 9.8 out of 10. The flaw is linked to CWE-74, or improper neutralization of special elements. This weakness can include command injection, operating system injection, and argument injection risks. 



 Cisco Patches Critical IOS XE Flaws 



 If successfully exploited, such weaknesses may allow an attacker to execute unintended commands or alter how a system processes input. Cisco also addressed CVE-2026-20267, an improper access control issue rated 9.0. 



 This vulnerability falls under CWE-284 and includes risks involving authentication bypasses, authorization failures, privilege issues, and other access-control weaknesses. Attackers could potentially abuse these conditions to gain access beyond their intended permissions. 



 Several other vulnerabilities received a maximum CVSS score of 8.6. CVE-2026-20268 involves memory buffer restrictions, including possible buffer overflows and out-of-bounds writes. 



 CVE-2026-20269 relates to improper resource lifetime management, such as invalid memory handling, null pointer dereferences, and file handler issues.

record.text: CISA Warns of TeamCity RCE Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks

external.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has warned that a critical JetBrains TeamCity flaw is being actively exploited. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-63077 , can let an unauthenticated attacker run code remotely on vulnerable TeamCity On-Premises servers. 



 CISA added the issue to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on August 5 and set an August 8 remediation deadline for affected federal civilian agencies. 



 TeamCity is a continuous integration and continuous delivery platform used to build, test, and deploy software. A compromise of its central server can create serious supply-chain risk. 



 Attackers may gain access to source code, build settings, stored secrets, signing material, and deployment connections. They could also alter build outputs or use the server as a foothold into a wider network. 



 The weakness is categorized as CWE-502, deserialization of untrusted data. It is part of the TeamCity agent polling protocol, which supports communication between build agents and the TeamCity server. 



 TeamCity RCE Vulnerability Exploited 



 According to the vulnerability description, a remote attacker with HTTP or HTTPS access can exploit the flaw to bypass authentication checks and execute operating system commands with the privileges of the TeamCity server process. No valid account is required. 



 JetBrains said all TeamCity On-Premises versions were affected before the security fixes. The company released patched versions 2025.11.7 and 2026.1.3. 



 Organizations that cannot upgrade immediately can use JetBrains’ security patch plugin on TeamCity 2017.1 and later. However, the plugin addresses only this vulnerability, so a full update remains the preferred long-term response. 



 TeamCity Cloud customers do not need to take any action, as the vendor has already implemented the required protections. CISA’s alert increases the urgency because it confirms exploitation in real attacks. 



 The agency has not publicly identified ransomware use for this specific issue, and its catalog entry lists that status as unknown. Even so, exposed CI/CD systems are high-value targets. 



 Threat actors have repeatedly targeted TeamCity vulnerabilities to obtain initial access, steal credentials, and move laterally across enterprise environments. 



 Administrators should first identify every TeamCity On-Premises installation, including development, testing, and disaster-recovery systems. 



 They should urgently update to a fixed release or deploy the vendor patch where an upgrade cannot be completed before the deadline. Security teams should restrict TeamCity access to trusted users, agents, and networks, removing unnecessary public exposure. 



 They should also review server and web logs for unusual agent polling activity, unexpected administrator actions, unfamiliar plugins, new accounts, and suspicious command execution. 



 Organizations should preserve relevant logs and system evidence before making major changes if compromise is suspected. They should rotate credentials, tokens, certificates, and other secrets stored or accessible through the platform, then inspect recent builds and release artifacts for unauthorized changes. 



 CISA also advises stakeholders to assess each asset’s internet exposure and follow its risk-based patching and forensic triage requirements. 



 Fast remediation is essential: unauthenticated remote code execution on a build server can quickly escalate into a full software supply chain incident. Monitoring should continue after remediation is complete.
